Predictive models must safely adapt to incoming patient data. In this paper, we introduce Balanced-Reservoir Replay (BRR), a simple modification to reservoir sampling that preserves minority-class examples when the buffer is full. We evaluated BRR on the eICU-CRD dataset (2,520 patients, 8.37% mortality) using only age and gender, in a task-incremental setup with eight tasks and buffer sizes ranging from 0 to 1000 samples.Using a 1000-sample buffer (~\u200940% of past data), BRR outperformed standard sequential training, achieving an average AUC of 0.628\u2009\u00b1\u20090.019 compared to 0.610\u2009\u00b1\u20090.016 (p\u2009<\u20090.01). It also reduced forgetting by 16% (0.106\u2009\u00b1\u20090.047 vs. 0.126\u2009\u00b1\u20090.066), which narrowed the gap with cumulative training by 39%. A clinical composite score, which penalized forgetting twice as much as accuracy gains (\u03bb\u2009=\u20092.0), indicated that a buffer size of 1000 was optimal. We conducted a sensitivity analysis of eight configurations of training duration (40 vs. 80 epochs per task) and forgetting penalties (\u03bb\u2009=\u20090.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0) supported the validity of this selection.This work questions the idea of minimal memory in continual learning. It indicates that retaining some past data can improve accuracy, enhance stability, and help meet regulatory requirements for slowly changing, low-data clinical tasks. BRR only needs about 50 KB of data, and it\u2019s easy to understand and use in places where resources are limited. for long-term time series forecasting are typically trained once and deployed as static predictors, despite operating in environments where data distributions continuously evolve. This mismatch between offline training and online deployment leads to progressive performance degradation and limits the practical adoption of modern forecasting models in real-world applications. To address this challenge, we formalize a continual learning (CL) for long-term time series forecasting problem, as a deployment-time adaptation problem and propose a model-agnostic framework enabling existing forecasting architectures to evolve without requiring storage of the entire historical dataset. Moreover we propose a new hybrid continual learning strategy that relies on a efficient use of knowledge distillation driven with a new attention-driven replay mechanism that continuously learns which historical sequences should be preserved for future adaptation, under memory constraints. Experiments conducted on state-of-the-art forecasting architectures, standard forecasting benchmarks, and real-world piezometric datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently improves forecasting accuracy while better preserving previously acquired knowledge than existing continual learning and adaptation strategies. Sequential optimization is difficult in this setting because it can distort both individual class representatives and their relative geometry, especially when vibration patterns also vary with operating conditions. We introduce graph continual prototype learning (GCPL), which represents each observed class by a prototype and connects related prototypes through a sparse feature-space graph. New-class samples initialize new nodes and local edges, whereas node- and edge-stability terms constrain changes to the previously learned class structure. The graph is learned from embeddings rather than predefined fault taxonomies, and its retained state scales with the number of classes instead of the number of vibration windows. A leakage-resistant evaluation protocol is specified for four public bearing datasets and jointly measures cumulative-class accuracy, old-class forgetting, new-class learning, and robustness to operating-condition shifts. This formulation provides a compact pattern-recognition framework for studying relational structure in replay-free incremental data with occasional distribution shifts, resulting in forgetting the information learned before each shift. Experience Replay (ER) addresses this challenge by retaining part of the old training samples and replaying them alongside current data, improving the model's understanding of the overall distribution in training batches. The crucial factor in ER performance is the diversity of samples within batches. The impact of sample diversity across a sequence of batches is investigated, introducing a new metric and an associated approach to assess and leverage this diversity. This exploration opens up significant potential for future work, as various strategies can be devised to ensure inter-batch diversity.
